parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a walking club to become a member.
script: Hello, I'd like to join the club, please.
Lovely. I'll fill in the form for you now. Can I have your name?
Michael Tennant. That's T, E, N, N, A, N, T.
That's right, and one at the end.
And what do you do, Michael?
I'm a nurse at the city hospital. I work shifts, which is partly why I want to join. I need something to help me relax.
Thanks. Now, we organise walks at three levels: beginner, intermediate and advanced. Have you done much walking?
I did a beginner's course last year, and I found it a bit easy towards the end. I don't think I'm ready for advanced, though, so I'll go for intermediate.
Good choice. The intermediate walks usually cover about fifteen kilometres. The beginner ones are about eight, and the advanced ones are often over twenty-five.
Most of our group walks take place on the first Sunday of every month. We used to meet on Saturdays, but too many members had work commitments.
We meet in the car park behind the museum on Castle Street. Some people go to the train station by mistake, but that's only for our summer coach trips.
Behind the museum. Got it. How much is membership?
It's twenty-eight pounds a year. It went up from twenty-five last year, I'm afraid, because of insurance costs.
That's still very reasonable. Are there any other benefits?
Yes, members get ten percent off at Peak and Valley, the camping shop on the high street. Their boots are excellent.
Great. Is there anything I should bring on my first walk?
The usual things: a waterproof jacket, water and snacks. And we strongly recommend a whistle. If you get separated from the group in fog, it's the easiest way to let people know where you are.
I'd never have thought of that. Thanks very much.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide speaks to passengers at the start of a boat trip through a mangrove forest.
script: Good morning, and welcome aboard the Mangrove Explorer. My name's Rafi, and I'll be your guide for today's trip through the mangrove forest. Before we leave the jetty, a few practical points.
The trip lasts about four hours, so we'll be back here at around one o'clock, not half past twelve, as it says in some of the older leaflets. The route was extended last year.
Lunch is included, and it'll be served on the boat, so there's no need to bring food. You may want to bring extra water, though, as it gets very hot on the upper deck.
For your safety, life jackets are under your seats. You don't need to wear them while you're sitting in the cabin, but please put one on if you go up to the open deck.

Now, a little about the forest itself. Mangroves are trees that grow in salt water along tropical coastlines. Their roots trap mud and protect the shore from storms. During cyclones, villages behind thick mangroves suffer far less damage than those without them. And of course, the forest is home to an amazing range of wildlife.

Let me tell you about the stops we'll make today. Our first stop is Heron Point. Despite its name, the real attraction there is the kingfishers. There are eight species in this area, and with luck you'll see several of them.
Next is Kotka Creek. At low tide, crocodiles often lie on the mud banks to warm themselves in the sun, so keep your cameras ready, but please stay inside the boat.

Our third stop is Kalabogi Station, where there's a wooden watchtower that you can climb. From the top, you can see right across the forest. People always ask about tigers. They do live here, but they're very rarely seen, so please don't be disappointed.
After that we'll call at Dublar Village. This is where local collectors bring the wild honey they gather from the forest, and you can buy it directly from them.
At Karamjal, there's a raised wooden path through the trees, so you can walk among the roots without getting your feet muddy.

Our final and longest stop is Hiron Lagoon. It's very peaceful there, and that's where we'll have lunch. Some people ask about swimming, but I'm afraid it isn't permitted anywhere on the trip, because of strong currents. Right, let's set off.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Maya and Ben, plan a survey of plastic on beaches.
script: So, Maya, we need to plan the methods section for our beach plastics project.
Right. First, which beaches to survey. I originally suggested three, but having looked at the bus timetables, I think two is more realistic.
I agree. What about the north beach?
That's the one near the river mouth, isn't it? I think we should definitely include it, because rivers carry a lot of plastic from inland.
The tourist beach at Sandy Bay. The comparison should be interesting: one where litter arrives from the river, and one where it's mostly left by visitors.
How about timing? I read that it's best to survey after a storm.

Actually, I'd say the opposite. Storms bring in huge amounts of material all at once, which would make our results unrepresentative. Let's go on calm days, at low tide, when more of the beach is exposed.
And we'll sort the plastic by type: bottles, bags, fishing gear, and microplastics?
Microplastics are going to be difficult without a microscope, and the lab's booked for the whole month. Let's leave them out and say so in our limitations.
OK. What surprised me in the reading was that fishing gear makes up such a large share of ocean plastic. Almost half, in some areas.
Me too. I'd assumed it would mostly be bottles and bags.
Right, so the procedure. First, we mark out a section of a hundred metres. How?
The sports department lends flags for orienteering. We could put one at each end.
Good. Then we walk across the section...
In parallel lines, about five metres apart, so we don't miss anything.
Everything larger than a fingernail. We'll sort items into separate buckets as we go, one for bottles, one for bags, and so on. I thought about using bags, but they'd tear.
Counting thousands of fragments would take forever. Weighing each category is much quicker, and it's what most published studies do.
Paper gets wet. I'll put everything straight into a spreadsheet on my tablet.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture about coral reefs and how scientists are trying to restore them.
script: Good morning. In today's lecture, I'll look at coral reefs: why they're in trouble, and what scientists are doing to restore them.

Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species. They're built by tiny animals called polyps, which live in partnership with algae. The algae provide the coral with food through photosynthesis, and they also give coral its bright colours.

When the water becomes too warm, even one degree above the normal summer maximum for a few weeks, this partnership breaks down. The coral expels the algae and turns white, a process known as bleaching. Bleached coral is not dead, but if high temperatures continue, it will starve.

So what can be done? The most common method of restoration is coral gardening. Small fragments of healthy coral are grown in underwater nurseries, often on structures made of plastic pipes, and then transplanted onto damaged reefs. The method works because many corals can grow from fragments. It's essentially a form of cloning.
However, coral gardening has limitations. It's slow and expensive. And if the new coral is genetically identical to the old, it may be just as vulnerable to heat.

This is why some researchers are trying selective breeding instead. In Australia, scientists collect coral from naturally warmer waters and breed it with coral from cooler reefs, hoping to produce young coral that can tolerate higher temperatures.

A third approach uses sound. Healthy reefs are noisy places, full of the clicks and grunts of fish and shrimp, while damaged reefs are quiet. In one experiment in Indonesia, researchers played recordings of healthy reefs through underwater speakers. The sound attracted young fish, which then helped to keep the reef clean.
But I want to emphasise one thing. None of these methods will succeed unless the underlying cause, rising ocean temperatures, is addressed. Restoration buys time. It isn't a solution in itself.

passages.title: How Honeybees Choose a New Home
paragraphs: Every spring, a healthy honeybee colony faces a dramatic decision. When the hive becomes crowded, the old queen leaves with around two-thirds of the workers, as many as 10,000 bees, to establish a new colony elsewhere. The swarm settles temporarily on a tree branch, hanging in a dense cluster, while it decides where to live. The choice matters enormously: a poor home may leave the colony unable to survive the winter.

Much of what we know about this process comes from the American biologist Thomas Seeley, who spent several decades studying honeybees. Some of his most important experiments took place on Appledore Island, off the coast of Maine. The island was ideal because it has almost no natural trees, so the bees had no choice but to consider the artificial nest boxes Seeley provided. By varying the size and shape of these boxes, he could test what the bees preferred.

The search is carried out by a few hundred older bees, known as scouts, which fly out in all directions looking for suitable cavities, usually in hollow trees. A good home, Seeley found, has a volume of around 40 litres and an entrance that is small, faces south and is several metres above the ground. Each feature has a purpose: a large cavity provides room to store enough honey for winter, a small entrance is easier to defend, and height offers protection from predators.

When a scout finds a promising site, it returns to the swarm and performs a 'waggle dance' on the surface of the cluster. The direction of the dance indicates the direction of the site in relation to the sun, while the length of the waggle indicates its distance. Crucially, the scout's enthusiasm reflects the quality of the site: a scout that has found an excellent cavity will repeat its dance many times, while one reporting an ordinary site will dance only briefly. Other scouts are recruited to inspect the advertised sites and, if impressed, begin dancing for them too.

Over several hours or days, support builds for the best sites, while weaker options lose their supporters, since scouts gradually stop dancing for any site. Remarkably, no individual bee compares the alternatives; most scouts visit only one site. The decision emerges from the competition between groups of dancers. When the number of scouts at one site reaches a threshold of around 20 to 30 bees present at the same time, they return to the swarm and produce a high-pitched 'piping' signal, which tells the other bees to warm up their flight muscles in preparation for take-off.

Seeley's experiments showed that the bees almost always choose the best available site. In one test, he offered five nest boxes, four of them ordinary and one excellent; the swarms chose the excellent box in four out of five trials. Seeley has argued that human groups could learn from this process, which he calls 'swarm intelligence'. In particular, he recommends that leaders avoid revealing their own preferences too early, encourage a wide search for options, and allow open debate before reaching a decision. He has even applied these principles when chairing meetings in his university department.

passages.title: Learning Something New at Any Age
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, scientists believed that the adult brain was essentially fixed. Children's brains were known to be highly adaptable, but it was assumed that after early adulthood the brain's structure stopped changing, and that learning a complex new skill, such as a musical instrument, a language or a sport, became steadily harder with age. Popular wisdom agreed: 'you can't teach an old dog new tricks'.

This view began to change in the 1990s and 2000s, thanks to new brain-imaging technology. In one well-known study published in 2000, researchers at University College London examined the brains of London taxi drivers, who must memorise the layout of around 25,000 streets to pass an exam known as 'the Knowledge'. The drivers had a larger posterior hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, than people in a control group, and the longer they had been driving, the larger it was. A later study followed trainee drivers over four years and found that the growth occurred only in those who passed the exam.

Similar changes have been observed in adults learning other skills. When volunteers in a German study spent three months learning to juggle, scans showed an increase in grey matter in areas of the brain that process visual motion. Strikingly, when they stopped practising, the increase partly disappeared. The brain, it seems, invests in skills that are being used and withdraws resources from those that are not, a principle sometimes summarised as 'use it or lose it'.

None of this means that age makes no difference. Children do appear to have advantages in some areas, notably in acquiring the pronunciation of a foreign language; adults who learn a language after their teenage years rarely sound exactly like native speakers. But adults have advantages of their own. They are generally better at understanding abstract rules, at planning their learning and at drawing on existing knowledge. In controlled studies over short periods, adult beginners often learn grammar and vocabulary faster than children.

Research on how people learn effectively has produced some surprising findings. One of the most reliable is the 'spacing effect': material studied in several short sessions spread over days is remembered far better than the same material studied in one long session. Another is the value of 'retrieval practice', which means testing yourself rather than simply re-reading notes. Learners themselves tend to prefer re-reading because it feels easier, but the very difficulty of recalling information seems to strengthen memory. The psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork have called these 'desirable difficulties'.

Perhaps the greatest obstacle for adult learners is not biological but psychological. Adults are used to feeling competent, and the experience of being a clumsy beginner can be uncomfortable, even embarrassing. Many give up in the early stages, interpreting slow progress as a sign that they lack talent. Researchers who study motivation suggest that learners who see ability as something that can grow through effort, which the psychologist Carol Dweck termed a 'growth mindset', are more likely to persist. The evidence on whether such mindsets can be taught is mixed, but the underlying message is supported by neuroscience: the adult brain remains capable of change throughout life.

passages.title: Drinking the Ocean
paragraphs: Water covers more than seventy percent of the Earth's surface, yet only about three percent of it is fresh, and most of that is locked in ice caps and glaciers. As populations grow and climate change alters rainfall patterns, some estimates suggest that by 2030 global demand for fresh water could exceed supply by forty percent. Faced with this prospect, a growing number of countries are turning to an apparently limitless source: the sea.

Desalination, the removal of salt from seawater, is not a new idea. Sailors in the ancient world boiled seawater and collected the steam, and the first large land-based plants, built in the 1950s and 1960s, used the same principle of distillation on an industrial scale. Distillation, however, requires enormous amounts of heat, and was practical mainly in the oil-rich countries of the Middle East, where energy was cheap.

The technology changed decisively with the development of reverse osmosis. In this process, seawater is pumped at very high pressure through membranes with pores so small that water molecules can pass through but salt cannot. Since the 1980s, improvements in membrane materials, and in devices that recover energy from the high-pressure waste stream, have cut the energy needed to produce a cubic metre of fresh water by more than eighty percent. Reverse osmosis now accounts for around seventy percent of global desalination capacity.

Today there are more than 20,000 desalination plants worldwide, supplying water to around 300 million people. Israel, once severely short of water, now obtains most of its household drinking water from five large coastal plants, and has gone from shortage to surplus within two decades. Singapore, which historically depended on water piped from neighbouring Malaysia, aims to meet thirty percent of its future needs through desalination. Even countries with periods of abundant rainfall, such as Australia and Spain, have built plants as insurance against drought.

Yet desalination remains controversial. The first concern is energy. Although efficiency has improved, removing salt from seawater still requires several times more energy than treating river water or groundwater, and where that energy comes from fossil fuels, desalination contributes to the very climate change that is making water scarcer. Some newer plants are powered by solar or wind energy, but these remain a minority.

The second concern is brine, the highly concentrated salt water left over after fresh water has been extracted. For every litre of fresh water produced, a typical plant generates about one and a half litres of brine, which is usually pumped back into the sea. Because brine is denser than seawater, it can sink and spread across the seabed, reducing oxygen levels and harming organisms that cannot move away, such as corals and seagrasses. In enclosed seas like the Persian Gulf, where many plants are concentrated and water circulates slowly, scientists have recorded rising salt levels near outflow pipes.

There are possible solutions. Diffusers, which are pipes with many small openings, can spread brine more widely so that it mixes quickly with seawater. Researchers are also exploring ways to turn brine into a resource by extracting valuable minerals such as magnesium and lithium, the latter in high demand for batteries. So far, however, extracting minerals from brine has proved too costly to be widely adopted.

Cost is the third issue. Desalinated water is typically two to three times more expensive than conventional supplies, which puts it out of reach for many of the poorest regions facing shortages. Critics argue that in many places the same money would achieve more if it were spent on repairing leaks, since some cities lose a third of their treated water through ageing pipes, or on recycling waste water. Desalination, they suggest, should be a last resort rather than a first choice.

Its supporters respond that, for coastal cities in dry regions, there may be no realistic alternative. As one engineer put it, the sea is the only reservoir that will never run dry. The challenge for the coming decades will be to make sure that, in solving one environmental problem, we do not create another.

task1.text: The table below shows how students at one university travelled to campus in 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The table shows the percentage of students at one university who used different types of transport to travel to campus in 2015 and 2025.

Overall, the most notable change was a sharp shift away from cars towards bicycles, while electric scooters emerged as a new option. By contrast, the proportions of students who took the bus or walked remained fairly stable.

In 2015, the car was the most common way of getting to campus, used by 35% of students, followed by the bus at 25% and walking at 20%. Only one in ten students cycled, and the same proportion used other forms of transport. Nobody used an electric scooter.

By 2025, the picture had changed considerably. The proportion of students driving had almost halved, to 18%, whereas cycling had more than doubled, to 24%, making it the most popular way to travel. Electric scooters accounted for 9% of journeys. Meanwhile, the figures for the bus and walking changed only slightly, to 22% and 21% respectively, and the share of other methods fell to 6%.

task2.text: Some people believe that university students should be free to study whatever subject they like. Others believe that they should only be allowed to study subjects that will be useful in the future, such as science and technology. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: The question of whether university students should choose their subjects freely or be directed towards practical fields has become more pressing as economies change rapidly. Although there are strong arguments for prioritising science and technology, I believe students should ultimately be free to choose.

Those who favour restricting choice argue that societies need certain skills to prosper. Countries that are short of engineers, doctors and software developers may struggle to compete, and graduates in these fields are usually more likely to find well-paid work. From this perspective, allowing large numbers of students to study subjects with fewer job opportunities wastes public money and leaves young people in debt without clear career prospects.

However, this view has serious weaknesses. Firstly, it is extremely difficult to predict which subjects will be 'useful' in twenty years. Skills that seem essential today may be automated tomorrow, while subjects such as psychology, design or languages can become unexpectedly valuable. Secondly, students who study something they are genuinely interested in tend to work harder and perform better. A reluctant engineering student is unlikely to become an outstanding engineer. Finally, society needs historians, artists and philosophers as well as scientists, because they help us understand ethical and cultural questions that technology alone cannot answer.

In my view, the best approach is to keep the choice with students while giving them clear information about career outcomes. Governments could also offer scholarships in fields where there are shortages, which would encourage students without forcing them.

In conclusion, although directing students towards science and technology may seem economically sensible, I believe freedom of choice, combined with good guidance, produces more motivated graduates and a more balanced society.

speaking.cue:
Describe a new skill you learned that you were proud of.
You should say:
- what the skill was
- how you learned it
- how long it took
and explain why you were proud of it.
speaking.cueModel: The skill I'd like to talk about is swimming, which might sound surprising, because a lot of people learn it as children. I grew up in a city, though, and I simply never had the chance. When I was about nineteen, some friends invited me on a trip to the beach, and I realised I'd be the only one who couldn't go into the water. That was the push I needed. I signed up for an adult beginners' course at a local pool, with two lessons a week. To be honest, the first few weeks were quite embarrassing. Most of the other learners were children, and I kept swallowing water. But the instructor was very patient, and she broke everything down into small steps: first floating, then kicking, then breathing. It took about three months before I could swim a full length without stopping. I was proud of it partly because it was physically hard, but mainly because I'd been scared of water for years, and I faced that fear. It also taught me that it's never too late to start something new, which is a lesson I've used in other areas of my life since then.
